READABILITY.evidence: Names say what they do (durabilityTracker, satisfiedLocked, failAllLocked, deliverLocked, positiveDuration). Public APIs have doc comments, and the subtle parts are commented, e.g. the floor/highest semantics and why waitJob never blocks. Short receivers like t, w and b are normal Go style.

MAINTAINABILITY.evidence: The dedicated durability.go (484 lines) is well split up. But it finds a user-set callback with a reflect pointer comparison against noopBatchDurable. It also spreads 8 durable* fields over batchInternal and couples Batch to DB through durableDB, so SyncWait has to call d.onBatchDurable.

ROBUSTNESS.evidence: All state is mutex-guarded, and the heap removes a waiter when its context is cancelled. Errors are latched, with firstErr and closedErr taking precedence. Limits are named constants (durabilityJobRetention, maxDurabilitySubscriptions), and errors are wrapped with errors.Wrapf/Safe. Job IDs at or below zero are rejected. No errors are swallowed.

C6-03-CASE1.evidence: API changes only add things. Non-sync commits gain only a couple of clock reads, and NoSyncWait commits are reported from SyncWait with no extra blocking. The tracker mutex is taken only on Sync commits, which already pay for an fsync. Existing callbacks are unchanged, and EnsureDefaults only adds the no-op hook.
